experiences.title: Topeka 1901: Agnes Ozman and 'Bible evidence'
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Parham's and Ozman's later accounts: Charles Parham had set his students to study what the Bible gave as evidence of the baptism of the Holy Spirit; they concluded it was speaking in tongues. On 1 January 1901 Agnes Ozman asked Parham to lay hands on her and began speaking what was believed to be Chinese, reportedly unable to speak English for several days. Parham and other students soon reported the same experience.

primarySource.title: Charles F. Parham, Kol Kare Bomidbar: A Voice Crying in the Wilderness (1902); Agnes Ozman LaBerge, What God Hath Wrought (c. 1921)
primarySource.citation: Parham 1902; Ozman's testimony in Apostolic Faith publications

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Parham taught that tongues were real foreign languages (xenolalia) given for end-time missions, so missionaries need not study languages; this expectation was not borne out and later Pentecostals generally reinterpreted tongues as prayer languages (glossolalia).

assessments.text: Topeka is where the 'initial evidence' doctrine was formulated; most Pentecostal histories treat it as a starting point, with Azusa Street as the decisive spread.
The failure of missionary xenolalia is cited as evidence that modern tongues are not the New Testament gift.

James Goff stresses Parham's role as the doctrinal founder of Pentecostalism; historians also note his later moral scandal (1907 arrest, charges dropped) and his racial views, which led him to denounce the interracial Azusa revival.
Studies of glossolalia (e.g. William Samarin, 1972) found it lacks the structure of natural language, while being a learnable, non-pathological religious behaviour.

experiences.story:
In the autumn of 1900 Charles Fox Parham, a 27-year-old independent Holiness preacher and faith healer, opened a small Bible school in Topeka, Kansas. It met in a rambling, unfinished mansion on the edge of town that locals called 'Stone's Folly'. Parham had grown up in Kansas, had briefly been a Methodist supply preacher, and had left denominational ministry convinced that God still healed the sick in answer to prayer. He charged no tuition; around forty students, many of them adults already in ministry, lived communally and 'by faith', with the Bible as their only textbook.

That summer Parham had travelled east to visit other Holiness centres, including Frank Sandford's community 'Shiloh' in Maine, where he heard reports of people speaking in unlearned languages. Like many in the Holiness movement he believed that a 'baptism of the Holy Spirit' was promised to believers after conversion, and he was searching for a clear, biblical sign that someone had received it. According to his own later account, in late December 1900 he set the students to study the Book of Acts on this question while he was away preaching. When he returned, he wrote, they had independently agreed that in each case in Acts the evidence was speaking in other tongues.

The school held a watch-night service on 31 December. On the evening of 1 January 1901, according to both Parham and Agnes Ozman, the 30-year-old Ozman, a former Midwest Bible-school student and city missionary, asked Parham to lay his hands on her and pray that she would receive the Spirit. She later wrote that as he prayed she began to speak in a language she did not know, and the group believed it was Chinese. Parham reported that for several days she could speak or write only in this tongue, and that she produced writing which they took to be Chinese characters.

Over the next few days Parham and a number of the other students reported the same experience. Parham later described the upper room of the school filled with students speaking what they believed were various human languages, including, they thought, Swedish, Russian, Bulgarian, Japanese and others. No linguist was present to examine these claims; the identifications were the participants' own.

Parham drew a bold conclusion. He taught that tongues were the 'initial evidence' of Spirit baptism and that the languages were real foreign tongues (later called xenolalia), given so that missionaries could preach to the nations without study in the short time left before Christ's return. Reporters from Topeka and Kansas City visited the school; some coverage was curious, some mocking. Early attempts by Parham's followers to use their tongues abroad did not produce the expected results, and later Pentecostals would generally understand tongues as prayer and praise in a language unknown to the speaker rather than as a missionary tool.

The immediate aftermath was disappointing. Parham's preaching tours drew little response, the school closed, and Stone's Folly was sold and later destroyed by fire. The movement revived in 1903 with a healing campaign in Galena, Kansas, and spread into Texas, where Parham opened a short-term school in Houston in December 1905. There a Black Holiness preacher, William J. Seymour, was allowed to listen to the lessons only from the hallway because of segregation. Seymour accepted Parham's teaching on tongues and carried it to Los Angeles in 1906.

Parham himself was soon sidelined. He broke with the Azusa Street Mission in late 1906, condemning its interracial worship and emotional excess, and in 1907 he was arrested in Texas on a morals charge that was later dropped but damaged his standing. He also promoted Anglo-Israelite ideas and, in later years, expressed sympathy for white-supremacist groups. Ozman married, joined the Assemblies of God and continued in ministry with her husband; her short memoir became a standard testimony in Pentecostal histories.

keyMoments.text: Charles Parham visits Holiness centres, including Frank Sandford's Shiloh community in Maine, and hears reports of speaking in unlearned languages.
Parham opens Bethel Bible School in 'Stone's Folly', a mansion in Topeka, Kansas.
Students study Acts and, by Parham's account, conclude that tongues are the biblical evidence of Spirit baptism.
Agnes Ozman asks Parham to lay hands on her and begins speaking in what the group believes is Chinese.
Parham and other students report speaking in tongues; reporters visit the school.
After a lean period, a healing revival in Galena, Kansas, revives Parham's Apostolic Faith movement.
At Parham's Houston school William J. Seymour, forced to sit outside the classroom, learns the tongues-as-evidence teaching.
Seymour carries the teaching to Los Angeles, where the Azusa Street revival begins.

experiences.significance: Topeka gave Pentecostalism its most distinctive doctrinal formula: that speaking in tongues is the 'initial evidence' of baptism in the Holy Spirit, a teaching still held by the Assemblies of God and many classical Pentecostal bodies. Because of this, many histories date the birth of Pentecostalism to 1 January 1901, although historians now stress multiple origins in India, Wales, Korea and Chile and the decisive role of Azusa Street. The episode also shows how belief can be revised in practice: the expectation of missionary xenolalia faded as tongues were reinterpreted as prayer languages. Critics, including many evangelicals and some Pentecostals, question the initial-evidence doctrine itself, and Parham's racism and later conduct remain a troubling part of the movement's founding story.

experiences.title: The Welsh Revival and Evan Roberts
experiences.account: Paraphrase of contemporary press reports (Western Mail; W.T. Stead) and Roberts' own statements: after an intense experience at Blaenannerch in September 1904, during which he prayed 'Bend me', 25-year-old former miner Evan Roberts returned home and began meetings at Moriah Chapel, Loughor, on 31 October 1904. Meetings lasted into the early morning with spontaneous prayer, hymn-singing in Welsh, confession and few sermons. Roberts urged four conditions: confess all known sin, remove anything doubtful, obey the Spirit promptly, and confess Christ publicly. Some 100,000 conversions were claimed within months; magistrates reported reduced drunkenness and crime.

primarySource.title: W.T. Stead, The Revival in the West (1905); Western Mail reports (1904-05)
primarySource.citation: Stead 1905; Western Mail 'Religious Revival in Wales' pamphlets (1904-05)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Supporters hailed it as a modern Pentecost; critics such as Rev. Peter Price (1905) attacked Roberts as a 'sham revival' leader. Roberts claimed visions and the ability to discern hidden sin in meetings, then collapsed from exhaustion in 1906 and withdrew, later co-writing War on the Saints (1912) with Jessie Penn-Lewis, which warned of deceptive spirits.

assessments.text: Remembered as the last great Welsh revival and a model of prayer-led, Spirit-led worship; many argue its moral fruit was real though short-lived in chapel attendance.
A direct precursor: Frank Bartleman corresponded with Roberts before Azusa Street, and many early British Pentecostal leaders (e.g. the Jeffreys brothers, Donald Gee's generation) were touched by it.
Some Reformed writers question its weak preaching and stress on immediate impressions, and point to Roberts' breakdown.
Eifion Evans and others link it to Welsh culture, the coal-mining society and pre-war religious anxiety; conversion numbers were real but chapel membership declined steadily after 1906.

debates: Roberts' claimed discernment and later breakdown.
experiences.story:
At the start of the twentieth century Wales was a land of chapels. Nonconformist denominations, especially the Calvinistic Methodists, Baptists and Independents, dominated religious life, and Welsh-language hymn-singing was part of everyday culture in the coal-mining valleys of the south. Yet many ministers worried that the fervour of earlier revivals, notably that of 1859, had cooled. In early 1904 a local awakening began at New Quay in Cardiganshire under the minister Joseph Jenkins, after a young woman, Florrie Evans, stood in a meeting and declared her love for Jesus; young people from New Quay began to carry the movement to other chapels.

Evan Roberts, born in 1878 in Loughor near Swansea, had gone down the pit as a boy and later trained as a blacksmith. Deeply devout, he had prayed for years for revival, and in 1904 he began preparing for the ministry at a school in Newcastle Emlyn. In late September 1904 he attended a meeting at Blaenannerch led by the evangelist Seth Joshua. According to Roberts' own account, when Joshua prayed that God would 'bend us', Roberts was overwhelmed and cried out 'Bend me'. He later described visions and an overwhelming sense of God's love in the weeks that followed, and a conviction that he must go home and speak to the young people of his own chapel.

On 31 October 1904 Roberts held a meeting at Moriah Chapel, Loughor, after the usual prayer meeting; only a handful of young people stayed. He urged them to accept four conditions: confess all known sin, put away anything doubtful, obey the Spirit promptly and confess Christ publicly. Night after night the numbers grew. Meetings ran until two or three in the morning, often without a sermon at all: people prayed aloud together, wept, confessed, and broke spontaneously into hymns. Roberts would sometimes sit silent for long periods, or walk the aisles. He was accompanied by a team of young women singers whose solos became part of the meetings.

Within weeks the movement spread through the valleys of Glamorgan and beyond, carried by Roberts' tours and by many other preachers and lay people. The Western Mail reported meetings daily and issued its reports as pamphlets; the London journalist W.T. Stead visited in December 1904 and described what he saw as a kind of spontaneous, leaderless worship. Contemporary reports told of chapels packed through the night, prayer meetings in the pits, public houses losing trade, and debts repaid. By early 1905 it was claimed that around 100,000 people had been converted, and magistrates in several districts commented on reduced drunkenness and crime. Some popular stories, such as pit ponies no longer understanding their drivers once they stopped swearing, belong to the revival's folklore.

Not everyone was persuaded. In January 1905 the Congregational minister Peter Price of Dowlais wrote to the Western Mail distinguishing what he saw as a genuine work of God in Wales from what he called a 'sham revival' centred on Roberts' personality and theatrical claims. Others were uneasy at Roberts' habit of announcing that someone present was resisting the Spirit, or at his refusal to preach in certain places. Supporters defended him vigorously. The controversy and the relentless pace began to tell on Roberts, who suffered periods of nervous exhaustion during 1905.

In 1906 Roberts withdrew from public life and went to live in Leicester with Jessie Penn-Lewis, a writer on the spiritual life, and her husband. With Penn-Lewis he later co-wrote War on the Saints (1912), which warned that believers could be deceived by evil spirits imitating the work of God, a book many read as a sober reflection on the revival's excesses. Roberts lived quietly for decades and died in Cardiff in 1951. The revival itself faded in Wales by 1906, but reports of it had already travelled to India, Korea, the United States and continental Europe.

keyMoments.text: At New Quay, Cardiganshire, Florrie Evans' public testimony sparks a local awakening among young people.
At a meeting led by Seth Joshua at Blaenannerch, Evan Roberts prays 'Bend me' and reports an overwhelming experience of God.
Roberts holds his first meeting with young people at Moriah Chapel, Loughor, and sets out his four conditions.
Meetings spread through the south Wales valleys and the Western Mail begins daily coverage.
W.T. Stead visits and publicises the revival to a British and international readership.
The Rev. Peter Price publicly criticises Roberts' role, sparking a press controversy.
Claims of some 100,000 conversions circulate, and news of the revival reaches India, Korea and Los Angeles.
An exhausted Roberts withdraws from public ministry to the home of Jessie Penn-Lewis in Leicester.

experiences.significance: The Welsh Revival was the most famous revival of its day and became a template for later movements: long, unstructured meetings, lay participation, public confession, and the expectation that God could 'come down' on a congregation. News of it fed directly into the Khasi Hills revival in north-east India, the Mukti revival, the 1907 Pyongyang revival and the expectant prayer groups in Los Angeles that preceded Azusa Street, so it is often counted among the forerunners of global Pentecostalism. Historians debate its lasting effect in Wales: chapel membership rose sharply but declined again within a decade, and secularisation continued. Roberts' later warnings about spiritual deception made the revival a lasting case study in discernment between genuine renewal, emotional contagion and personality-centred enthusiasm.

experiences.title: The Mukti revival under Pandita Ramabai
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Mukti Prayer-Bell reports and Minnie Abrams' account: after Ramabai organised daily prayer for revival among the young widows and orphans in her care, on 29-30 June 1905 girls at the Mukti Mission reported seeing fire and being 'baptised with fire': many wept, confessed sins, shook, prayed aloud for hours and some fell into trances or saw visions. By late 1906 some were speaking in tongues, including, it was reported, languages they had not learned.

primarySource.title: Mukti Prayer-Bell (Mukti Mission newsletter, 1905-07); Minnie F. Abrams, The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire (1906)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Ramabai, a Marathi Brahmin scholar turned Christian reformer, interpreted the revival as the Spirit's answer to prayer and an Indian-led renewal. News of Mukti reached Los Angeles and Chile (through Abrams' pamphlet to Willis Hoover), contributing to the global Pentecostal network independent of Azusa.

assessments.text: Allan Anderson and others cite Mukti as evidence that Pentecostalism had multiple origins, not only in North America.
Ramabai is honoured as a Bible translator (Marathi) and champion of women; the revival is valued for repentance and social care, with some caution about manifestations.
Historians note the revival's context: Brahmin widowhood, famine orphans and Indian Christian nationalism; Ramabai resisted Western missionary control.
At the time some Hindu reformers accused Ramabai of using her mission to convert vulnerable girls, a controversy that shaped her reputation in India.

experiences.story:
Pandita Ramabai (1858-1922) was one of the most remarkable Indian women of her age. Born into a Marathi Brahmin family and taught Sanskrit by her father, she was honoured with the title 'Pandita' by scholars in Calcutta in 1878 for her learning. Widowed young with a small daughter, she became an outspoken campaigner for the education of women, especially child widows, who were often treated as outcasts. In England in 1883 she was baptised in the Anglican Church, though she remained independent-minded about denominational theology.

Back in India she opened a home and school for high-caste widows, the Sharada Sadan, in Bombay and later Pune. During the terrible famines of 1896-97 and 1899-1900 she travelled into stricken districts and brought hundreds of starving girls and young women to her farm at Kedgaon, near Pune, which she named Mukti ('liberation' or 'salvation'). By the early 1900s Mukti housed around two thousand residents, with schools, workshops, farms and a printing press, and was largely run by Indian women.

Ramabai had heard reports of revivals in Australia, Wales and the Khasi Hills of north-east India. In January 1905, according to the Mukti Prayer-Bell, she invited volunteers to meet daily to pray for an outpouring of the Spirit on India; several hundred young women joined prayer circles that met twice a day. An American Methodist missionary, Minnie Abrams, who led the Bible school at Mukti, worked closely with her.

The reports describe how, at the end of June 1905, the revival broke out. During the night of 29-30 June one girl was said to have been seen with something like fire around her, so that another girl ran for water to put it out, before realising there was no physical fire. Many of the residents wept, confessed their sins, trembled, prayed aloud for hours and spoke of being 'baptised with fire'. Some fell into trances or reported visions of Christ. Abrams and Ramabai reported that ordinary work was set aside for days at a time, and that bands of young women went out to villages around Kedgaon to preach.

By late 1906 some of the girls were speaking in tongues. Mukti reports claimed that a few spoke languages they had not learned, including English and Greek, alongside unknown tongues; these claims were reported by the mission and not independently tested. Ramabai welcomed tongues as a gift but did not teach that they were the necessary evidence of the Spirit, emphasising instead repentance, love and service. Some missionaries elsewhere in India were sceptical of the emotional scenes and worried about disorder among young, vulnerable residents; Ramabai and Abrams defended the revival as an Indian work of God.

News travelled quickly. Abrams' booklet The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire (1906) circulated widely, and a copy reached Willis Hoover, the Methodist missionary in Valparaíso, Chile, whose congregation experienced a similar revival in 1909 that gave birth to Chilean Pentecostalism. Reports from Mukti were also printed in the Azusa Street mission's newspaper. Ramabai continued her work for decades, completing a translation of the Bible into colloquial Marathi from the original languages shortly before her death in April 1922.

keyMoments.text: Ramabai is baptised in the Anglican Church while studying in England.
During famine in western India Ramabai brings destitute girls to Kedgaon and founds the Mukti Mission.
Ramabai calls for daily prayer for revival; hundreds of young women join prayer circles.
Residents report being 'baptised with fire', with weeping, confession, trembling and visions.
Minnie Abrams publishes The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire, spreading news of the revival.
Some Mukti girls begin speaking in tongues, including, the mission reported, unlearned languages.
Abrams' booklet helps inspire the Methodist revival in Valparaíso, Chile, that begins Chilean Pentecostalism.
Ramabai dies shortly after completing her Marathi Bible translation.

experiences.significance: The Mukti revival is a key piece of evidence that Pentecostal-type Christianity had several centres of origin and was not simply exported from North America; it was led by an Indian woman and carried out largely by Indian girls and women. Through Abrams' writings it shaped revival in Chile and fed the global Holiness-Pentecostal network that Azusa Street joined. Ramabai is also honoured as a pioneer of women's education and social reform in India, and is commemorated in the Anglican and Episcopal calendars. Critics and historians raise questions about religious fervour among dependent and traumatised young women, and about conversion in mission institutions, while others see in Mukti an early example of indigenous Christian leadership challenging missionary control.

experiences.title: Azusa Street Mission, Los Angeles
experiences.account: Paraphrase of The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles, 1906-08) and Frank Bartleman's 1925 memoir: in April 1906, prayer meetings led by the African American Holiness preacher William J. Seymour at 214 Bonnie Brae Street saw people speak in tongues and fall under the power; the meetings moved to a former AME church at 312 Azusa Street. Services ran almost continuously for three years, with Black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers, women leaders, tongues, healings and people 'slain' on the floor. Bartleman wrote that 'the color line was washed away in the blood.' The Los Angeles Times mocked it as a 'Weird Babel of Tongues' (18 April 1906).

primarySource.title: The Apostolic Faith (newspaper of the Azusa Street Mission), 1906-08; Frank Bartleman, How Pentecost Came to Los Angeles (1925)
primarySource.citation: The Apostolic Faith 1:1 (September 1906); Bartleman 1925; Los Angeles Daily Times, 18 April 1906

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Participants saw a restoration of Pentecost before Christ's return; missionaries left for Africa, Asia and Europe within months. Parham visited in October 1906 and denounced what he saw as fanaticism and racial mixing; the mission later split, and Seymour's congregation became mostly Black.

assessments.text: Azusa Street is the iconic birthplace of global Pentecostalism, whose interracial, egalitarian beginnings are celebrated as a sign of the Spirit's work.
Critics from B.B. Warfield onward argued modern tongues and healings are not the apostolic gifts; some describe Azusa as emotional excess.
Many Holiness leaders (e.g. Alma White, the Pillar of Fire) denounced the revival as 'the last vomit of Satan'; the movement divided Holiness churches.
Cecil M. Robeck Jr. documents the revival's racial and social dynamics; Allan Anderson stresses that Azusa was one of several centres (Wales, Mukti, Pyongyang, Chile).

debates: Race and the interracial ideal (and its collapse).
Seymour vs. Parham on leadership and discernment.
experiences.story:
Los Angeles in 1906 was a booming, multi-ethnic city with many Holiness missions whose members were praying for a revival like the one they had read about in Wales. Into this setting came William Joseph Seymour, born in 1870 in Centerville, Louisiana, to parents who had been enslaved. Seymour had lost the sight of one eye to smallpox, had joined the Holiness movement, and in Houston in early 1906 had attended Charles Parham's Bible school, forced by segregation to listen from the hallway. There he accepted Parham's teaching that speaking in tongues was the evidence of Spirit baptism, although he had not yet experienced it himself.

Invited to Los Angeles to preach at a small Holiness mission led by Julia Hutchins, Seymour arrived in February 1906, but when he preached on tongues the door was locked against him. He began holding prayer meetings in the home of Richard and Ruth Asberry at 214 North Bonnie Brae Street. On 9 April 1906, according to participants, Edward Lee and then others began speaking in tongues; Seymour himself reported the experience a few days later. Crowds gathered on the street, and the porch reportedly collapsed under the weight of people.

Within days the group rented a dilapidated former African Methodist Episcopal church building at 312 Azusa Street, recently used as a warehouse and stable. With planks laid on boxes for pews and two shoe-crates as a pulpit, meetings began and ran almost continuously, often three times a day, for the next three years. The congregation was strikingly mixed: Black and white, Latino, Asian and European immigrants, rich and poor, with women as well as men leading prayer and preaching. Seymour often prayed with his head inside one of the crates. Participants described tongues, singing in the Spirit, healings, people falling to the floor and long periods of silence.

The Los Angeles Daily Times of 18 April 1906 mocked the meetings under the headline 'Weird Babel of Tongues', describing them as a scene of fanaticism. The same day the San Francisco earthquake struck, and many in the mission saw it as a sign of the last days. Frank Bartleman, a white Holiness journalist who attended, later wrote in his 1925 memoir that at Azusa 'the color line was washed away in the blood'. In September 1906 the mission began publishing The Apostolic Faith, which soon reached tens of thousands of readers worldwide.

Visitors came from across North America and beyond and carried the experience home: Gaston B. Cashwell to the American South, Charles H. Mason to the Church of God in Christ, William Durham to Chicago, and missionaries who left within months for Liberia, Angola, India, China and Japan. Critics were many. Older Holiness leaders denounced tongues as delusion or worse, and newspapers ridiculed the meetings.

The bitterest criticism came from Parham himself. Arriving in October 1906, he condemned what he saw as fanaticism, hypnotic influences and the mixing of Black and white worshippers, and he tried unsuccessfully to take control. Further divisions followed. In 1908 Florence Crawford and Clara Lum moved to Portland, Oregon, taking the newspaper's national mailing list with them, and in 1911 William Durham tried to take over the mission while promoting a different view of sanctification. Seymour, who had married Jennie Evans Moore in 1908, continued to lead a smaller, mostly African American congregation until his death in 1922.

The interracial ideal soon gave way to the colour lines of American society: within a decade many white Pentecostals had formed separate denominations, such as the Assemblies of God in 1914. Yet the movement launched at Azusa Street had already spread around the world, and the mission is remembered by Pentecostals everywhere as the place where their movement came of age.

keyMoments.text: William J. Seymour arrives in Los Angeles to preach at Julia Hutchins' Holiness mission, but is soon locked out.
At prayer meetings at 214 North Bonnie Brae Street, participants begin speaking in tongues.
The meetings move to a former AME church building at 312 Azusa Street.
The Los Angeles Daily Times mocks a 'Weird Babel of Tongues'; the San Francisco earthquake strikes the same day.
The mission begins publishing The Apostolic Faith, which spreads news of the revival worldwide.
Charles Parham visits, condemns the meetings and breaks with Seymour.
Florence Crawford and Clara Lum move to Portland with the newspaper's mailing list.
William Durham attempts to take over the mission, leading to further division.
Seymour dies in Los Angeles; the mission declines and the building is later demolished.

experiences.significance: Azusa Street was the most important single hub in the early spread of Pentecostalism, which with the later charismatic movements now numbers several hundred million people worldwide. It gave the movement a newspaper, a network of missionaries, and a story of origins in which a Black preacher led a racially mixed, Spirit-filled congregation, a story that later Pentecostals have drawn on in efforts at racial reconciliation. Historians debate how far it was the 'origin' of Pentecostalism, since similar revivals were occurring in India, Wales, Korea and Chile, and how quickly its interracial ideal was abandoned. Critics then and now question the emotional phenomena and the doctrine of tongues as evidence, while admirers see Azusa as a modern Pentecost that reshaped world Christianity.

experiences.title: The Pyongyang Great Revival
experiences.account: Paraphrase of missionary reports (Graham Lee, William Blair) in The Korea Mission Field (1907): during a winter Bible conference in January 1907, on the evenings of 14-15 January, after an invitation for many to pray aloud at once, the congregation broke into simultaneous audible prayer, weeping and public confession of sins including theft, hatred and adultery; some fell to the floor in agony. Elder Gil Seon-ju (Kil Sun-ju) confessed to embezzling money from a deceased friend's estate. The movement spread through Korea's churches and schools.

primarySource.title: The Korea Mission Field (1907); William Blair and Bruce Hunt, The Korean Pentecost and the Sufferings Which Followed (1977, incl. Blair's earlier account)
primarySource.citation: Graham Lee, 'How the Spirit Came to Pyeng Yang', Korea Mission Field, March 1907; Blair & Hunt 1977

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Missionaries called it the 'Korean Pentecost'. It shaped distinct Korean practices: tongsong kido (praying aloud together), daybreak prayer (saebyeok kido, associated with Gil Seon-ju) and intensive Bible study. Japanese colonial pressure (protectorate 1905, annexation 1910) formed the background.

assessments.text: Regarded as the spiritual foundation of Korean Christianity's growth; its centenary in 2007 was widely celebrated.
Cited as one of the global revivals of 1904-07 alongside Wales and Azusa, though it was not characterised by tongues.
Scholars debate whether missionaries encouraged the revival partly to depoliticise Korean Christians under Japanese rule; others stress its indigenous agency and confession culture.
Collective weeping and confession are analysed as cathartic responses to national humiliation and social stress.

experiences.story:
Protestant Christianity had come to Korea only in the 1880s, through American Presbyterian and Methodist missionaries, but it grew quickly, especially in the northern city of Pyongyang. The missionaries adopted the 'Nevius method', which stressed self-supporting, self-governing churches and intensive Bible study by ordinary believers. The years after 1900 were a time of national humiliation: Japan defeated Russia in 1905 and imposed a protectorate on Korea that November, ending its control of its own foreign affairs. Many Koreans looked to the churches as places of education, community and hope.

A first stirring of revival came in 1903 at Wonsan, where the Canadian Methodist medical missionary Robert Hardie publicly confessed his pride and failures to his Korean congregation, prompting others to confess too. In 1906 the missionaries in Pyongyang, having heard reports of the revivals in Wales and in the Khasi Hills of India, began meeting to pray for a similar outpouring. A visiting speaker, Howard Agnew Johnston, told them about these movements in the autumn of 1906.

In January 1907 about 1,500 men gathered in Pyongyang for the annual winter Bible class, centred on the Jangdaehyun (Central) Presbyterian Church. According to the missionary Graham Lee's account in The Korea Mission Field, on the evening of 14 January, after a short sermon, he invited the congregation to pray, and so many began to pray at once that he told them all to pray aloud together. The result, he wrote, was a great volume of simultaneous prayer, like the sound of many waters, as hundreds poured out their hearts. People wept, cried out and confessed sins publicly; some fell to the floor, beating it with their fists in distress.

The next evening, 15 January, the confessions continued. Missionaries recorded admissions of theft, hatred, adultery and even hatred of the Japanese, alongside quarrels between Christians. The most remembered confession came from Gil Seon-ju (Kil Sun-ju), a respected elder, who said he had taken money from the estate of a deceased friend whose affairs he had promised to manage, and that he would repay it to the widow. William Blair later described these nights as overwhelming, with the meetings continuing into the early hours.

The movement spread rapidly through Pyongyang's churches and schools, including Union Christian College and girls' schools, and then to Seoul and other cities as students and church leaders travelled home. Missionaries called it the 'Korean Pentecost'. It shaped lasting habits of Korean Protestantism: tongsong kido, praying aloud together; daybreak prayer meetings, associated with Gil Seon-ju; and deep commitment to Bible study and evangelism. In 1907 the first Korean Presbyterian ministers were ordained, Gil among them.

Contemporaries and later historians have also asked harder questions. Some Korean scholars argue that the missionaries, anxious to keep churches out of politics under Japanese rule, encouraged an inward, individual piety that turned believers away from national resistance. Others point out that many revival leaders later took part in the independence movement: Gil Seon-ju was one of the 33 signers of the March First Declaration of 1919. Public confession has been praised as cleansing and criticised as potentially coercive.

keyMoments.text: Robert Hardie's public confession at Wonsan sparks a smaller revival among Korean Methodists.
Japan imposes a protectorate on Korea after the Russo-Japanese War.
Pyongyang missionaries pray for revival after hearing reports from Wales and India.
About 1,500 men gather for the winter Bible class at Jangdaehyun Church, Pyongyang.
Graham Lee invites everyone to pray aloud together, and simultaneous prayer, weeping and confession break out.
Elder Gil Seon-ju publicly confesses misusing a dead friend's estate; confessions continue through the night.
The revival spreads to schools and churches across Korea; the first Korean Presbyterian ministers are ordained.
Gil Seon-ju is among the 33 signers of the March First Declaration of Korean independence.

experiences.significance: The 1907 revival is often called the spiritual birth of Korean Protestantism, which became one of the most vigorous churches in Asia and a major sender of missionaries. Its practices of praying aloud together, early-morning prayer and lay-led Bible study remain hallmarks of Korean churches worldwide. Pyongyang, once called the 'Jerusalem of the East', is now the capital of North Korea, where open Christian practice is severely restricted, which gives the memory of 1907 a poignant weight for Korean Christians. Historians continue to debate the revival's political meaning under colonial rule and whether it depoliticised or strengthened Korean Christian nationalism.

experiences.title: Fátima and the 'Miracle of the Sun'
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Lúcia's later Memoirs and 1917 press reports: from 13 May to 13 October 1917 three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto, report monthly appearances of a lady 'brighter than the sun' calling for prayer of the rosary and penance for the end of the war. On 13 October 1917 a crowd estimated at 30,000-70,000, including journalists from the anticlerical paper O Século, saw (by many accounts) the sun spin, change colour and appear to plunge toward the earth; some present saw nothing unusual.

primarySource.title: Lúcia dos Santos, Memoirs (written 1935-1941 and later); O Século report by Avelino de Almeida, 15 October 1917
primarySource.citation: Memoirs I-IV; O Século, 15 October 1917; pastoral letter of the Bishop of Leiria (1930)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Republican Portugal's anticlerical authorities briefly detained the children in August 1917. The Bishop of Leiria declared the visions worthy of belief in 1930. The 'three secrets' (Lúcia wrote them down 1941-44; the third was published by the Vatican in 2000) linked the apparitions to hell, Russia's conversion and the persecution of the Church, and became central to Cold War Catholic piety.

assessments.text: An approved apparition; Francisco and Jacinta were canonised in 2017. The Vatican's 2000 commentary (Cardinal Ratzinger) interpreted the third secret symbolically and stressed that private revelation adds nothing to public revelation.
Generally reserved, especially about messages concerning the 'consecration of Russia'.
Usually sceptical of the Marian messages; some accept that witnesses saw an unusual phenomenon without accepting its interpretation.

Witness reports vary greatly; proposed explanations include optical effects from staring at the sun and collective expectation. Much of the detailed content of the visions comes from Lúcia's memoirs written two decades later.

debates: Later-written secrets and their political use.
experiences.story:
In 1917 Portugal was a deeply Catholic rural country governed by an anticlerical republic. The revolution of 1910 had overthrown the monarchy, separated church and state, expelled religious orders and restricted public worship. Portugal had entered the First World War in 1916, and Portuguese soldiers were fighting in Flanders. Fátima was a small parish in the hills of central Portugal, where families lived by farming and herding sheep.

The three visionaries were cousins: Lúcia dos Santos, aged ten, and Francisco and Jacinta Marto, aged eight and seven. According to Lúcia's later Memoirs, written from 1935 onwards, they had already in 1916 seen an angel who taught them prayers, though she did not speak of this at the time. On 13 May 1917, while grazing sheep at the Cova da Iria, they reported seeing a lady 'brighter than the sun' standing above a small holm oak. Only Lúcia spoke with her and heard her; Jacinta saw and heard; Francisco said he only saw. The lady asked them to return on the 13th of each month, to pray the rosary every day for peace and the end of the war, and to make sacrifices for sinners.

News spread quickly, despite Lúcia's mother's scepticism and the parish priest's caution. Growing crowds came on 13 June and 13 July. On 13 July the lady is said to have shown the children a vision of hell and to have entrusted them with a secret; its content, as Lúcia later wrote it, also spoke of devotion to the Immaculate Heart of Mary and of Russia. In August the local administrator, Artur de Oliveira Santos, took the children into custody for two days and threatened them in an effort to make them reveal the secret or admit to a hoax; they refused. They reported a further apparition on 19 August at Valinhos, and again at the Cova on 13 September.

The children said the lady had promised a miracle in October so that all would believe. On 13 October 1917, after a morning of heavy rain, a crowd variously estimated at 30,000 to 70,000 had gathered. Many present, including the journalist Avelino de Almeida of the anticlerical Lisbon daily O Século, reported that when the clouds parted the sun appeared as a pale disc that could be looked at, seemed to tremble or spin, threw off colours and appeared to plunge toward the earth before returning to its place; some said their soaked clothes were suddenly dry. Other observers saw nothing unusual, and accounts differ in detail. Lúcia said that she had seen the Holy Family and other visions in the sky, and that the lady had named herself 'the Lady of the Rosary'.

Francisco and Jacinta both died in the influenza pandemic, in 1919 and 1920. Lúcia was sent to school with the Dorothean sisters and later became a Carmelite nun in Coimbra, where she lived until her death in 2005. After a canonical inquiry, the Bishop of Leiria declared on 13 October 1930 that the visions were worthy of belief and authorised the cult of Our Lady of Fátima.

Much of what is now known as the 'message of Fátima' comes from Lúcia's Memoirs written decades later, including the angel apparitions and the first two parts of the secret, published in the early 1940s. The third part, written in 1944, was kept by the Vatican and published only in 2000, with a commentary by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger interpreting it as a symbolic vision of the Church's sufferings in the twentieth century, including the 1981 attempt on John Paul II's life. Sceptics have explained the sun phenomena as optical effects of looking at the sun through thinning cloud, shaped by expectation, and have questioned how much of the later material reflects 1917; Catholic teaching treats the apparitions as private revelation that the faithful are not obliged to believe.

keyMoments.text: Lúcia, Francisco and Jacinta report seeing a radiant lady above a holm oak at the Cova da Iria.
The children say they were shown a vision of hell and given a secret.
The local administrator detains the children and pressures them to reveal the secret.
A crowd of tens of thousands reports seeing the sun spin and plunge; others see nothing unusual.
Francisco dies in the influenza pandemic; Jacinta follows in February 1920.
The Bishop of Leiria declares the apparitions worthy of belief.
Lúcia writes down the first two parts of the secret in her Memoirs; the third is written in 1944.
The Vatican publishes the third secret with a theological commentary by Cardinal Ratzinger.
Pope Francis canonises Francisco and Jacinta Marto at Fátima on the centenary.

experiences.significance: Fátima became one of the most visited Marian shrines in the world and a central symbol of twentieth-century Catholic devotion, shaping rosary piety, devotion to the Immaculate Heart, and papal consecrations of the world and of Russia by Pius XII and John Paul II. Its anti-communist reading made it powerful in Cold War Catholicism, and John Paul II connected his survival of the 1981 assassination attempt to Our Lady of Fátima. Historians and critics note the role of later memoirs in forming the message and the political uses made of it, including under Portugal's Estado Novo, while Protestant and Orthodox Christians generally do not accept such apparitions as revelation. Catholic authorities continue to stress that private revelations, however approved, add nothing binding to the faith.

experiences.title: Padre Pio's stigmata at San Giovanni Rotondo
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Padre Pio's letter to his superior (22 October 1918): on 20 September 1918, praying before a crucifix in the friary choir, the Capuchin friar Pio of Pietrelcina saw a mysterious figure with bleeding hands, feet and side, and found the same wounds on himself; they bled for the next fifty years. Devotees attributed to him healings, prophetic knowledge of penitents' sins and bilocation.

primarySource.title: Padre Pio, Letters (Epistolario), vol. 1
primarySource.citation: Letter to Padre Benedetto of San Marco in Lamis, 22 October 1918; medical reports of Luigi Romanelli (1919) and Giorgio Festa

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Doctors examined the wounds with conflicting conclusions; Fr Agostino Gemelli, physician and Franciscan, judged them suspect. The Holy Office restricted Pio's public ministry several times (1923, 1931-33) and investigated him again under John XXIII. Paul VI lifted restrictions; John Paul II canonised him in 2002.

assessments.text: One of the most popular modern saints; the stigmata are widely believed to be supernatural, though canonisation rests on his heroic virtue and attested miracles, not on the wounds as such.
Mostly sceptical; some respect his austere piety while rejecting stigmata and bilocation claims as unproven.

Sergio Luzzatto's study discusses archival allegations (e.g. a 1919 purchase of carbolic acid) and the political uses of Pio's cult in Fascist and post-war Italy; supporters dispute these interpretations.
Skeptics propose self-inflicted or psychosomatic wounds; no independent medical study during his lifetime settled the question.

debates: Natural vs. supernatural explanations of stigmata.
experiences.story:
Francesco Forgione was born in 1887 in Pietrelcina, a farming village near Benevento in southern Italy. Pious from childhood, he entered the Capuchin Franciscans at fifteen, taking the name Pio, and was ordained priest in 1910. Chronically ill with fevers and stomach complaints, he spent years living with his family rather than in a friary. In letters to his spiritual directors from this period he described intense spiritual struggles, visions, attacks by demons and, from around 1910, invisible pains in his hands and feet.

In 1916 he was sent to the small friary of Our Lady of Grace at San Giovanni Rotondo, an isolated town on the Gargano peninsula in Apulia. In August 1918 he described a mystical experience of being pierced in the heart, which he and his directors called a 'transverberation'. Then, on 20 September 1918, while praying alone in the friary choir before a crucifix after Mass, he reported seeing a mysterious figure with bleeding hands, feet and side. When the vision ended, he wrote to his superior Padre Benedetto on 22 October 1918, he found that his own hands, feet and side were pierced and bleeding, and he begged God to take away the visible signs while leaving the pain.

Word spread through the region after the end of the First World War, and crowds began to come to see the friar, attend his Mass and confess to him. Devotees reported that he could read their consciences, that his wounds gave off a sweet perfume, that people were healed through his prayers, and that he had appeared to people far away (bilocation). His Mass could last for hours, and penitents waited days for confession.

Doctors who examined the wounds reached different conclusions. Luigi Romanelli, examining him in 1919, reported deep lesions he could not explain; the Roman pathologist Amico Bignami suggested a superficial necrosis that might have been maintained by chemical irritants; Giorgio Festa, sent by the order, described them as unexplained. In 1920 the Franciscan physician and psychologist Agostino Gemelli visited and, although he was not permitted a full examination, judged the case to be one of suggestion and self-inflicted wounds. Later historians, notably Sergio Luzzatto, drew on Vatican archives showing that a local pharmacist had testified in 1919 that Pio had asked her for carbolic acid and veratrine; Pio's defenders replied that carbolic acid was used to sterilise syringes.

The Holy Office was cautious. In 1923 it declared that the supernatural character of the phenomena had not been established and restricted his public ministry, and from 1931 to 1933 he was barred from saying public Mass or hearing confessions. The restrictions were later lifted, and his following grew. With donations from admirers around the world he built a large hospital, the Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza, opened in 1956, and promoted prayer groups that spread internationally. Under John XXIII a further apostolic visitation in 1960 examined the friary's finances and Pio's relations with devotees.

Padre Pio died on 23 September 1968; according to witnesses the wounds had faded and were no longer visible at his death. John Paul II, who as a young priest had visited him in 1947, beatified him in 1999 and canonised him in 2002. San Giovanni Rotondo became one of the largest pilgrimage centres in Italy, and his image is found throughout the Catholic world.

keyMoments.text: Pio is ordained a priest and begins describing invisible pains in his hands and feet in letters to his directors.
He is assigned to the friary at San Giovanni Rotondo in Apulia.
Praying in the choir before a crucifix, he reports a vision and finds bleeding wounds on his hands, feet and side.
He describes the event in a letter to his superior, Padre Benedetto.
Agostino Gemelli visits and judges the stigmata to be the product of suggestion or self-infliction.
The Holy Office declares the supernatural character unproven and restricts his ministry; further restrictions follow 1931-33.
The Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza hospital, funded by his followers, opens in San Giovanni Rotondo.
Padre Pio dies; witnesses report the wounds had disappeared.
John Paul II canonises him as St Pio of Pietrelcina.

experiences.significance: Padre Pio became the most famous stigmatic of modern times and one of the most popular saints in Catholicism, with prayer groups, a major hospital and a pilgrimage centre bearing his name. His story illustrates the Catholic Church's two-sided approach to extraordinary phenomena: decades of suspicion and restriction by the Holy Office, followed by canonisation based on his life of prayer and charity and on investigated miracles rather than on the stigmata themselves. Critics and historians have raised natural explanations, including self-inflicted wounds, and have examined the commercial and political dimensions of his cult. Protestant and sceptical observers generally view stigmata through psychological or medical lenses, while his devotees regard him as a living image of Christ crucified.

experiences.title: Kathryn Kuhlman's 'miracle services'

place.name: Carnegie Hall and First Presbyterian Church, Pittsburgh

experiences.account: Paraphrase of Kuhlman's I Believe in Miracles (1962): after a woman testified in 1947 (in Franklin, Pennsylvania) to being healed of a tumour during Kuhlman's preaching, without any prayer for her, Kuhlman's services became famous for healings announced from the platform by 'word of knowledge' rather than by prayer lines. Many who came forward fell backward 'under the power' when she prayed. From 1948 she held services in Pittsburgh, later at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles and on national television.

primarySource.title: Kathryn Kuhlman, I Believe in Miracles (1962)
primarySource.citation: Kuhlman 1962; William A. Nolen, Healing: A Doctor in Search of a Miracle (1974)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Kuhlman insisted she had no healing power and credited the Holy Spirit; her ministry crossed denominational lines and helped prepare the Charismatic Renewal, including among Catholics.

assessments.text: Regarded as a pioneer whose emphasis on the Holy Spirit's sovereignty, rather than the healer's faith, influenced later figures such as Benny Hinn.
Cessationists cite the absence of verifiable organic healings and her personal controversies as evidence against modern healing gifts.

The surgeon William Nolen followed up people claimed as healed at a 1970s Kuhlman meeting and reported that he could not confirm any organic cures; some were harmed by abandoning treatment. Supporters reply that sample selection was limited.
David Harrell places her within the post-war healing revival but notes her greater respectability and appeal to mainline and Catholic audiences.

debates: Celebrity and finances in healing ministries.
experiences.story:
Kathryn Kuhlman was born in 1907 in Concordia, Missouri, and began preaching as a teenager, travelling with her sister and brother-in-law on the revival circuit in the American West. In the 1930s she built a successful independent ministry in Denver, the Denver Revival Tabernacle. In 1938 she married Burroughs Waltrip, an evangelist who had divorced his wife; the scandal cost her most of her following, and after some years she left the marriage and began rebuilding her ministry in smaller towns.

In 1946 she settled in Franklin, Pennsylvania, preaching and broadcasting on radio. According to her own account in I Believe in Miracles (1962), the turning point came in 1947, when at one of her services a woman stood up and testified that during Kuhlman's preaching the evening before she had been healed of a tumour, without anyone praying for her. Kuhlman said she had been searching for an understanding of healing that did not depend on the evangelist's power, and she took this as a sign that the Holy Spirit himself healed, sovereignly, during worship and preaching.

In 1948 she moved to Pittsburgh, holding services first at the Carnegie Hall auditorium in the North Side and later at the First Presbyterian Church downtown. Her meetings had a distinctive style. There were no healing lines or healing cards. Instead, during the service she would announce, by what she described as a word of knowledge, that someone in a certain part of the hall was being healed of a particular condition, and invite them to come forward and testify. As she prayed over those who came, many fell backward 'under the power', a phenomenon later known as being slain in the Spirit. Her flowing white dresses, dramatic voice and insistence that she was 'nothing' and the Spirit was everything became her trademarks.

From 1965 she also held regular services at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles, and from the late 1960s her television programme, also called I Believe in Miracles, was broadcast nationally. Her meetings attracted Catholics, mainline Protestants and Pentecostals alike, and she was warmly received in the emerging charismatic renewal; in 1972 she met Pope Paul VI. The Kathryn Kuhlman Foundation supported missions and charitable work.

Critics questioned the healing claims. The most influential critique came from the Minnesota surgeon William A. Nolen, whose book Healing: A Doctor in Search of a Miracle (1974) followed up people who had claimed healing at a Kuhlman meeting in Minneapolis in the early 1970s. He reported finding no cases of cure of organic disease that he could confirm, and some cases of harm, including a woman with cancer of the spine who discarded her brace and suffered a collapsed vertebra. Kuhlman's supporters pointed to other documented testimonies and argued that medical follow-up of a small sample was not decisive. Toward the end of her life she also faced lawsuits and disputes with former staff over finances.

Kathryn Kuhlman died in Tulsa on 20 February 1976 after heart surgery. Among those who later claimed her influence was the healing evangelist Benny Hinn, who said her meetings shaped his ministry.

keyMoments.text: Kathryn Kuhlman is born in Concordia, Missouri.
Her marriage to the divorced evangelist Burroughs Waltrip causes a scandal and the collapse of her Denver ministry.
In Franklin, Pennsylvania, a woman testifies to being healed of a tumour during Kuhlman's preaching.
Kuhlman moves to Pittsburgh and begins services at Carnegie Hall, North Side.
She begins regular services at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles.
She meets Pope Paul VI, reflecting her standing in the charismatic renewal.
Surgeon William Nolen publishes Healing, reporting no medically confirmed cures among the people he followed up.
Kuhlman dies in Tulsa after heart surgery.

experiences.significance: Kathryn Kuhlman was one of the best-known women preachers of the twentieth century and a bridge between classical Pentecostal healing revivalism and the cross-denominational charismatic renewal, including among Catholics. Her model of 'sovereign' healing announced by words of knowledge, and of people falling under the power, shaped later healing ministries such as Benny Hinn's and much charismatic practice. Nolen's study became a standard reference in debates over whether healing claims can or should be medically verified, and over the risks of people abandoning treatment. Her life also raises questions about women's leadership in churches that restricted it, and about celebrity, finances and accountability in independent ministries.

experiences.title: Oral Roberts' tent healing crusades
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Roberts' autobiographical accounts: healed of tuberculosis and stuttering as a teenager (1935), the Pentecostal Holiness preacher Oral Roberts launched healing campaigns in 1947 from Tulsa. In a huge tent seating thousands, he laid hands on long 'healing lines' of the sick, often praying against demons and disease. From 1955 his crusades were filmed for television, bringing Pentecostal healing into American living rooms.

primarySource.title: Oral Roberts, Expect a Miracle: My Life and Ministry (1995); Healing Waters / Abundant Life magazine (1947-)
primarySource.citation: Roberts 1995; campaign reports in Healing Waters

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Admirers saw a restoration of apostolic healing; journalists and doctors questioned unverified cures. Roberts later founded Oral Roberts University (1963), joined the United Methodist Church (1968) and taught 'seed faith' giving, an early form of prosperity theology. His 1987 appeal that God would 'call him home' unless he raised $8 million drew widespread criticism.

assessments.text: A key bridge from classical Pentecostalism to the Charismatic Renewal and televangelism; many credit his ministry with physical and spiritual healing.
His move into Methodism symbolised growing mainline openness to charismatic practice, though many mainline clergy were critical of his methods.
Critics such as John MacArthur challenge prosperity teaching and unverifiable healing claims.
David Harrell's biography shows a complex figure who moved from the tent revival to institution-building; historians link his 'seed faith' to the rise of the prosperity gospel.

experiences.story:
Granville Oral Roberts was born in 1918 near Ada, Oklahoma, the son of a poor Pentecostal Holiness preacher; his mother had Choctaw ancestry. As a boy he stammered badly. At seventeen, in 1935, he collapsed with tuberculosis, which had killed relatives. According to his own often-repeated testimony, his brother took him to a tent revival in Ada, where the evangelist prayed for him; he said that he was healed of both the tuberculosis and the stammer that night, and that he heard God tell him he would take the message of healing to his generation.

For the next twelve years Roberts was a Pentecostal Holiness pastor and evangelist in Oklahoma, Georgia and North Carolina, and studied briefly at college. In 1947, while pastoring in Enid, Oklahoma, he reported being struck by the verse 3 John 2, with its wish that the reader 'prosper and be in health', and became convinced that God wanted people well and prosperous. He resigned his pastorate, held a healing meeting in Enid in May 1947, and moved to Tulsa, which became his base for the rest of his life. He began a magazine, Healing Waters (later Abundant Life), and a radio programme.

The campaigns grew quickly. Roberts bought a large tent, and by the 1950s his 'tent cathedral' could seat well over ten thousand people. The style was direct and physical. After a long sermon on faith, Roberts would sit at the front while a 'healing line' of the sick passed before him, sometimes for hours; he laid his right hand on each person and prayed, often commanding diseases and demons to leave. He encouraged a 'point of contact', an act of faith such as touching the radio or the magazine. In 1950 a windstorm in Amarillo, Texas, collapsed the tent during a service, but no one was killed, which supporters took as a sign of protection.

Roberts was one of the leading figures of the post-war 'healing revival' of the late 1940s and 1950s, alongside William Branham, Jack Coe, A.A. Allen and others associated with Gordon Lindsay's Voice of Healing network. In 1955 he began filming his crusades for television, showing the healing lines in American homes for the first time. Many viewers wrote in with testimonies; others were shocked. Journalists, doctors and some church leaders challenged the healing claims as unverified and accused him of exploiting the desperate. A 1956 crusade in Melbourne, Australia, was disrupted by hostile crowds and press criticism and ended early.

Roberts was less sensational than some of his colleagues and avoided the scandals that destroyed others. As the tent era waned in the 1960s he moved toward respectability: he founded Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, chartered in 1963, and in 1968 joined the United Methodist Church, to the dismay of many Pentecostals. He developed the teaching of 'seed faith', that gifts to God's work are seeds that God will multiply back to the giver, which became a foundation of later prosperity theology.

His later ventures drew more controversy. He built the City of Faith medical centre in Tulsa, opened in 1981 to combine prayer and medicine, which struggled financially and closed in 1989. In 1987 he told supporters that God would 'call him home' if he did not raise eight million dollars for medical scholarships; the money was raised, but the appeal was widely mocked and criticised. Roberts died in 2009, aged 91; his son Richard succeeded him and later resigned as university president in 2007 amid a financial scandal.

keyMoments.text: Seventeen-year-old Oral Roberts reports being healed of tuberculosis and stammering at a tent revival in Ada, Oklahoma.
Inspired by 3 John 2, he holds his first healing campaign in Enid and soon moves his ministry to Tulsa.
His tent campaigns grow rapidly, with long healing lines and the magazine Healing Waters.
A windstorm collapses his tent in Amarillo, Texas, without fatalities.
Roberts begins televising his healing crusades nationally.
Oral Roberts University is chartered in Tulsa.
Roberts joins the United Methodist Church.
His appeal that God would 'call him home' unless he raised $8 million draws national criticism.
Roberts dies in California aged 91.

experiences.significance: Oral Roberts brought Pentecostal healing out of rural tents and into mainstream American life through television, a university and his move into Methodism, helping make Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity respectable and paving the way for the charismatic renewal in older churches. His 'seed faith' teaching is widely regarded as a seedbed of the prosperity gospel, now influential across Africa, Latin America and Asia as well as the United States. Critics, including many evangelicals and Pentecostals, fault the lack of verification of healings, the financial appeals and the theology linking giving to material reward. Admirers stress his role in democratising prayer for the sick and in building lasting institutions.

experiences.title: William Branham and the post-war healing revival
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Branham's own accounts and campaign literature: Branham said that on 7 May 1946 an angel appeared to him and commissioned him to take a gift of healing to the world, with a sign of vibrations in his left hand that revealed diseases, and later the ability to discern people's names and secrets. His 1946-55 campaigns drew vast crowds in North America, Europe, South Africa and India. A 1950 photograph in Houston was promoted as showing a supernatural light above his head.

primarySource.title: Gordon Lindsay, William Branham: A Man Sent from God (1950); The Voice of Healing magazine (1948-)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Branham is often regarded as the catalyst of the 1946-58 'Voice of Healing' revival, which included Oral Roberts, Jack Coe and A.A. Allen. In later years he taught the 'serpent seed' doctrine, baptism in Jesus' name only (Oneness theology) and his own role as an end-time Elijah; these teachings separated him from most Pentecostal churches. His followers ('Message' believers) remain numerous, especially in Africa.

assessments.text: Many credit his early ministry with genuine healings and prophetic accuracy, while rejecting his later doctrines; he is a cautionary example of gifting without sound teaching.
His Oneness, serpent-seed and self-prophetic teachings are seen as heretical or cultic; his story is used to argue that miracles do not validate doctrine.
C. Douglas Weaver's study analyses Branham's charisma and the healing revival's mass-media methods; historians also note documented failed prophecies and contested healing claims.
Regard him as the prophet of the last church age whose recorded sermons carry special authority.

debates: Miracles vs. doctrine as a test of a prophet (cf. Deuteronomy 13).
experiences.story:
William Marrion Branham was born in 1909 in a log cabin near Burkesville, Kentucky, into a very poor family that soon moved to Jeffersonville, Indiana, across the Ohio River from Louisville. In his later sermons he told of supernatural experiences from childhood: a light that appeared at his birth, and a voice from a whirlwind in a tree telling him not to drink, smoke or defile his body. Researchers have since noted that several of these autobiographical stories changed over time and are hard to corroborate. As a young man he was converted, ordained in an independent Baptist setting, and in 1933 began a small independent church in Jeffersonville, the Branham Tabernacle. In 1937 his wife and baby daughter died, a tragedy he described as a punishment for having refused, on others' advice, to associate with Pentecostals.

According to Branham, on 7 May 1946, while he was praying alone, an angel appeared and told him he had been sent to take a gift of divine healing to the peoples of the world. The angel promised two signs: a vibration in his left hand when he held a sick person's hand, revealing the disease, and later the ability to know the 'secrets of the heart'. Within weeks he held meetings in St Louis and among Oneness Pentecostals in the American South and West, where crowds reported dramatic healings.

From 1947 Gordon Lindsay became his campaign manager and in 1948 founded The Voice of Healing magazine to publicise the meetings. Branham's style was quiet and unpolished, in contrast to many evangelists. He would call people forward and, according to admirers, tell them details of their lives and illnesses before praying. His campaigns from 1946 to the mid-1950s drew huge crowds across North America and, from 1950, in Scandinavia, Britain, South Africa (1951), India (1954) and elsewhere. Reported healings included that of the former congressman William Upshaw, who said in 1951 that he could walk after decades of disability.

In January 1950, during a debate in Houston between Branham's associate F.F. Bosworth and a Baptist critic, a photographer hired by the critic's side took a picture showing a band of light above Branham's head. A document examiner, George Lacy, reported that the negative had not been retouched; Branham's followers have presented the photograph ever since as a picture of a supernatural light, while sceptics attribute it to lighting or a processing artefact.

Critics raised doubts at the time and later. Observers noted that people declared healed sometimes died soon afterwards, and that claims of raising the dead and of cures were rarely documented. The historian C. Douglas Weaver, among others, has examined the gap between Branham's accounts and the evidence. Branham's campaigns declined from the mid-1950s, and he faced a long dispute with the US tax authorities over his finances.

In his later years, preaching mostly at Jeffersonville, Branham developed teachings that separated him from most Pentecostals: the 'serpent seed' doctrine (that Eve's sin involved sexual union with the serpent, producing Cain's line), baptism in Jesus' name only, rejection of the doctrine of the Trinity as usually stated, condemnation of denominations as the mark of the beast, and strict rules on women's dress and roles. Many of his followers came to see him as the end-time prophet in the spirit of Elijah promised in Malachi 4. He predicted major end-time events around 1977. On 18 December 1965 his car was struck by a drunk driver in Texas, and he died on 24 December.
