He founds the Branham Tabernacle in Jeffersonville, Indiana.
Branham reports an angelic visitation commissioning him to a worldwide healing ministry.
His first major healing meetings in St Louis draw large crowds.
Gordon Lindsay founds The Voice of Healing magazine to promote Branham's campaigns.
A photograph taken in Houston showing a light above his head is promoted by followers as supernatural.
He campaigns in South Africa; the former congressman William Upshaw claims healing.
Branham dies of injuries from a car crash in Texas on 18 December.

experiences.significance: Branham is widely seen as the catalyst of the post-war American healing revival, and his style of 'word of knowledge' and discernment influenced later charismatic and Latter Rain movements and many healing evangelists. His later teachings, rejected by mainstream Pentecostals and outside Nicene Trinitarian orthodoxy, gave rise to the 'Message' movement, whose followers remain numerous, especially in Africa and Latin America. For critics he is a cautionary example of how reported miracles can lend authority to aberrant doctrine, often discussed with reference to Deuteronomy 13 and Matthew 7:22-23. Historians use his career to examine personality cults, the lack of accountability in independent healing ministries and the reliability of self-told life stories.

experiences.title: Lights over the church at Zeitoun, Cairo

place.name: Church of St Mary, Zeitoun, Cairo

experiences.account: Paraphrase of press and church reports: from the night of 2 April 1968, Muslim mechanics working opposite the Coptic Orthodox Church of St Mary in Zeitoun reported a luminous female figure on the church dome. Over the next two to three years crowds, Christian and Muslim, numbering in the tens of thousands on some nights, reported luminous figures, glowing 'doves' and lights; photographs were published, and healings were claimed.

primarySource.title: Statement of the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate (4 May 1968); Egyptian press reports, April-May 1968
primarySource.citation: Patriarchal statement under Pope Cyril VI (Kyrillos VI), 4 May 1968

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Pope Cyril VI's commission declared the apparitions authentic in May 1968, and many Egyptians read them as consolation after the 1967 war. The Zeitoun site, believed to lie on the route of the Holy Family's flight into Egypt, became a major pilgrimage centre.

assessments.text: Accepted as genuine appearances of the Theotokos, celebrated annually; seen as a sign of God's care for Egypt's Christians.
Catholic observers reported positively at the time, but the Vatican has issued no formal judgement since it was not a Catholic site.
Generally sceptical of Marian apparitions, while some accept that unusual lights were observed.
Proposed explanations include tectonic strain or earthquake lights (Derr and Persinger, 1989), reflections, and mass expectation; others suspected projection, though no evidence of this was found.

debates: Natural explanations for collectively observed lights.
experiences.story:
Zeitoun (al-Zaytun) is a district in north-eastern Cairo. Its Coptic Orthodox Church of St Mary was built in the 1920s; according to a local tradition, the family that endowed it had been told in a dream that the Virgin Mary would one day appear there. The area is also associated in Coptic tradition with the route of the Holy Family's flight into Egypt. The Coptic Church, Egypt's ancient Christian community, was led from 1959 by Pope Cyril VI (Kyrillos VI), a monk known for his prayer and reports of healings. In June 1967 Egypt suffered a crushing defeat by Israel in the Six-Day War, a national trauma for Muslims and Christians alike.

On the night of 2 April 1968, according to the earliest reports, workers at a public-transport garage across the street from the church, Muslims, saw what looked like a woman in white on the dome of the church. Thinking she might be about to jump, they shouted to her and called for help; a crowd gathered, and some cried out that it was the Virgin Mary. One of the workers was later said in popular accounts to have been healed of an injured finger. The figure was reported to have disappeared after a few minutes.

In the following weeks the reports multiplied. On many nights, often after midnight, crowds that grew to tens of thousands, Christians and Muslims together, gathered in the streets around the church. Witnesses described a luminous figure of a woman, sometimes kneeling or bowing toward a cross on the dome, sometimes holding a child; bird-like shapes of light flying over the church; clouds of incense-like vapour; and flashes of light. Photographs were taken and published, some showing a bright glowing form above the dome. Many healings were claimed, and pilgrims reported conversions and deep emotion.

Pope Cyril VI appointed a committee of clergy to investigate, and on 4 May 1968 the Coptic Patriarchate issued a statement declaring that the Virgin Mary had appeared over the church. Egyptian newspapers reported the events widely, and according to press accounts police and authorities searched the surrounding area for any device that could project an image and found none. The state media and tourism authorities gave the events considerable publicity. The reports continued, with decreasing frequency, until around 1970-71.

Interpretations varied. For Copts the apparitions were a sign of the Virgin's protection of Egypt and of their ancient church; many Muslims, who honour Maryam in the Qur'an, also venerated the sight. Some Egyptians read them as divine consolation after the defeat of 1967. The anthropologist Cynthia Nelson, studying the events, emphasised their meaning as a collective response to national crisis. Sceptics proposed natural explanations: some researchers, notably John Derr and Michael Persinger, linked the lights to luminous phenomena associated with tectonic strain, while others suggested reflections, street lighting or the power of expectation in a crowd. Critics also noted the political usefulness of the events to the government after 1967.

Zeitoun became a major pilgrimage centre, and the date of the first apparition is commemorated by the Coptic Church. The Catholic Church, which has no jurisdiction over the Coptic Orthodox Church, made no official judgement. Similar reports of lights over Coptic churches occurred in later decades, for example in the Shubra district of Cairo in 1986.

keyMoments.text: Egypt is defeated in the Six-Day War, a national trauma.
Muslim transport workers opposite St Mary's Church, Zeitoun, report a luminous woman on the church dome.
Crowds of tens of thousands gather nightly; witnesses report luminous figures, 'doves' of light and healings.
After an investigation ordered by Pope Cyril VI, the Coptic Patriarchate declares the apparitions authentic.
Photographs of lights over the dome are published in the Egyptian and international press.
Reported apparitions become rare and cease around this time.
Similar reports of lights over a Coptic church in Shubra, Cairo, revive interest in Zeitoun.

experiences.significance: Zeitoun is the most famous modern Marian apparition in the Orthodox world and an unusual case in which Muslims as well as Christians were among the principal witnesses, giving it interreligious significance in Egypt. It strengthened Coptic identity and pilgrimage at a time of political and social pressure and is remembered as a sign of the Virgin's protection over Egypt. For sceptics and social scientists it is a key case study in collectively observed lights, crowd expectation and the political context of religious phenomena. It also shows differences in how churches handle such events: the Coptic Patriarchate pronounced quickly, whereas Catholic procedure is typically slower, and Protestants generally do not regard such apparitions as revelation.

experiences.title: The Toronto Blessing: holy laughter and 'soaking'

place.name: Toronto Airport Vineyard (now Catch the Fire), Toronto

experiences.account: Paraphrase of participants' and observers' accounts: on 20 January 1994 the Missouri Vineyard pastor Randy Clark, recently touched at meetings of the South African evangelist Rodney Howard-Browne, began meetings at John and Carol Arnott's Toronto Airport Vineyard. Congregants laughed uncontrollably ('holy laughter'), fell to the floor, shook, wept and, controversially, sometimes roared or made animal-like sounds. Nightly meetings continued for years, drawing hundreds of thousands of visitors from around the world, many of whom carried the 'blessing' to their home churches (e.g. Holy Trinity Brompton, London).

primarySource.title: Contemporary accounts by participants (e.g. Guy Chevreau, Catch the Fire, 1994) and sociological fieldwork
primarySource.citation: Margaret Poloma, Main Street Mystics (2003); Chevreau 1994

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Supporters spoke of refreshing and renewal rather than revival proper, emphasising the Father's love. In December 1995 John Wimber's Association of Vineyard Churches withdrew its endorsement, citing manifestations given excessive prominence and unbiblical interpretation; the church became Toronto Airport Christian Fellowship.

assessments.text: Many testify to deep renewal, healing of emotional wounds and missionary fruit (e.g. Heidi and Rolland Baker's Iris Ministries in Mozambique); defenders cite Edwards and Wesley to argue manifestations are secondary to fruit.
Critics such as Hank Hanegraaff (Counterfeit Revival, 1997) argued the phenomena were induced by suggestion and lacked biblical warrant; others warned against experience-centred worship.
Some charismatic Anglicans and Catholics embraced the 'blessing'; others counselled discernment and integration with sacramental life.
Margaret Poloma's surveys found many participants reported lasting positive changes; scholars analyse the role of expectation, music and group dynamics in inducing bodily manifestations.

debates: Renewal vs. revival; fruit vs. phenomena.
experiences.story:
The Vineyard movement, led by the Californian pastor John Wimber, had since the 1980s promoted 'power evangelism' and expected signs and wonders in ordinary church life. In 1993 the South African evangelist Rodney Howard-Browne drew attention in the United States, especially at meetings in Lakeland, Florida, where uncontrollable laughter ('holy laughter') and falling were common. Randy Clark, pastor of a Vineyard church in St Louis, attended Howard-Browne's meetings and reported being renewed. John and Carol Arnott, pastors of the small Toronto Airport Vineyard, meeting in a strip-mall unit near Pearson Airport, had been seeking renewal themselves, and in late 1993 visited meetings in Argentina led by Claudio Freidzon.

The Arnotts invited Clark to lead four days of meetings beginning on Thursday, 20 January 1994. According to participants, on the first night, as Clark prayed for the roughly 120 people present, many fell to the floor, laughed uncontrollably, wept or shook. The meetings were extended, then extended again, and soon ran six nights a week. Within months they had become a destination for visitors from across North America and the world.

The characteristic manifestations included laughter, falling and lying on the floor for long periods ('carpet time'), shaking, jerking, appearing 'drunk in the Spirit', and weeping. Most controversially, some people roared like lions, crowed or made other animal-like sounds, which some leaders interpreted as prophetic signs. The Arnotts emphasised that the core message was the Father's love, and that the phenomena were not the goal; they spoke of 'refreshing' or 'renewal' rather than revival.

In May 1994 Eleanor Mumford, a leader in the British Vineyard, described the Toronto meetings to staff at Holy Trinity Brompton, a large Anglican church in London, and similar scenes followed there. A British journalist dubbed the phenomenon the 'Toronto Blessing', and the name stuck. Thousands of churches in Britain, Europe, Asia and Africa reported similar experiences, often through pastors who had visited Toronto. The church claimed hundreds of thousands of visitors within a few years.

Opposition was sharp. Many evangelical and Reformed critics argued that the phenomena lacked biblical warrant, that they resembled hypnotic or crowd-induced states, and that animal noises in particular were bizarre or worse; the American broadcaster Hank Hanegraaff's Counterfeit Revival (1997) was one of the most forceful attacks. Others compared the events to earlier revivals, such as those under Jonathan Edwards and John Wesley, which had also seen bodily phenomena, and argued that they should be judged by their fruit.

John Wimber himself became uneasy. Concerned that the manifestations were being given too much prominence and interpreted without biblical support, the board of the Association of Vineyard Churches withdrew its endorsement in December 1995. The church became the Toronto Airport Christian Fellowship, and later Catch the Fire. The sociologist Margaret Poloma, who surveyed visitors, found that many reported lasting effects such as greater love for God and others, a deeper prayer life and involvement in ministry to the poor. Meetings continued for years, and the church still hosts conferences.

keyMoments.text: Randy Clark is touched at Rodney Howard-Browne's 'holy laughter' meetings; John and Carol Arnott visit Claudio Freidzon in Argentina.
Clark begins meetings at the Toronto Airport Vineyard; many laugh, fall and shake on the first night.
Meetings are extended indefinitely and begin running six nights a week.
Eleanor Mumford brings the experience to Holy Trinity Brompton in London.
The British press coins the name 'Toronto Blessing'.
The Association of Vineyard Churches withdraws its endorsement of the Toronto church.
The church is renamed Toronto Airport Christian Fellowship, later Catch the Fire.
Hank Hanegraaff publishes Counterfeit Revival, a sharp critique of the movement.

experiences.significance: The Toronto Blessing was one of the most widely spread charismatic renewals of the late twentieth century, touching thousands of churches, including many Anglican and Baptist congregations in Britain, and feeding into the Brownsville revival, Bethel Church in Redding, and the work of Heidi and Rolland Baker's Iris Ministries in Mozambique. It renewed debate about bodily manifestations in revival, the role of emotion and suggestion, and how to discern spiritual experiences, echoing eighteenth-century arguments over the Great Awakening. Critics saw it as excess or deception that divided congregations; supporters and some sociological research point to lasting changes in prayer, compassion and ministry among participants. The Vineyard's withdrawal remains a notable case of a movement setting limits on its own revival.

experiences.title: The Brownsville (Pensacola) Revival

place.name: Brownsville Assembly of God, Pensacola, Florida

experiences.account: Paraphrase of church and press reports: on Father's Day, 18 June 1995, evangelist Steve Hill, recently prayed for at Holy Trinity Brompton in London, preached at Brownsville Assembly of God (pastor John Kilpatrick). Hundreds came forward; many fell, shook or jerked. Meetings continued four or five nights a week until about 2000; the church claimed some 2.5 million visitors and well over 100,000 recorded 'decisions'. Unlike Toronto, the emphasis was on repentance and conversion with Hill's urgent preaching.

primarySource.title: Brownsville Assembly of God reports; John Kilpatrick, Feast of Fire (1995)
primarySource.citation: Kilpatrick 1995; Pensacola News Journal investigative series (November 1997)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Assemblies of God leaders largely endorsed the revival as authentic. A 1997 Pensacola News Journal series questioned the planning of the original outbreak, the revival's finances and the manifestations; leaders disputed its conclusions. A ministry school trained students for missions.

assessments.text: Widely regarded as one of the largest US revivals of the late 20th century, emphasising holiness and evangelism.
Critics such as Hank Hanegraaff argued the manifestations were induced and the theology shallow.
The Pensacola News Journal series alleged the 'spontaneous' outbreak had been anticipated and raised questions about money and statistics; supporters countered with testimonies of transformed lives.
Placed in the wave of 1990s 'renewal' revivals linked through Holy Trinity Brompton and Toronto, but with a distinctly classical Pentecostal, repentance-centred style.

experiences.story:
Brownsville Assembly of God was a well-established Pentecostal congregation in a working-class district of Pensacola, Florida. Its pastor, John Kilpatrick, had led it since 1982 and, from around 1993, led the church in Sunday-evening prayer meetings for revival. The congregation had heard of the Toronto Blessing and of renewal at Holy Trinity Brompton in London. Like many Assemblies of God churches, it looked back to the Azusa Street revival as its spiritual heritage, and its members hoped to see something similar in their own day. Kilpatrick later said that he had been through a period of personal discouragement and had felt that the church needed a fresh visitation of God rather than new programmes.

Steve Hill, an Assemblies of God evangelist who had served as a missionary in Argentina and elsewhere, had a dramatic personal testimony of deliverance from drug addiction. In 1995 he visited Holy Trinity Brompton and received prayer from its vicar, Sandy Millar, an experience he said renewed him. Kilpatrick invited him to preach at Brownsville on Father's Day, 18 June 1995.

According to the church's accounts, after Hill's morning sermon he invited people to come forward for prayer, and something unusual happened: hundreds responded, many falling to the floor, shaking or weeping. Kilpatrick himself reportedly fell and lay on the platform for hours. The evening service continued in the same way. Hill stayed on, and the meetings were extended from week to week.

Meetings settled into a pattern of four or five nights a week, Wednesday to Saturday, with Sunday-morning services. Unlike Toronto, Brownsville's emphasis was on repentance and conversion: Hill preached urgent, often loud sermons against sin and called people to 'run to the altar'. Worship, led by Lindell Cooley, was long and intense, and many people shook, jerked or fell. Visitors queued from early morning for seats; the church reported baptisms of thousands and testimonies of people leaving drugs, alcohol and crime. Over five years the church claimed some 2.5 million visitors and well over 100,000 recorded decisions for Christ. The Brownsville Revival School of Ministry, led by the theologian Michael Brown from 1997, trained students for evangelism and missions.

In November 1997 the Pensacola News Journal published an investigative series questioning parts of the story: it reported that Kilpatrick had predicted a revival in advance, that aspects of Hill's testimony were exaggerated, that the bodily manifestations followed recognisable patterns, and that substantial revenue from offerings, books and recordings flowed to the ministry and its leaders. The leaders strongly disputed the series. The Assemblies of God leadership, including its General Superintendent Thomas Trask, endorsed the revival as genuine, while critics such as Hank Hanegraaff included it in their attacks on contemporary revivalism.

By 2000 the meetings were winding down. Hill left to start a church in Texas; a dispute between the church and the leadership of the ministry school led Brown and others to form a separate school; and Kilpatrick left Brownsville in 2003. Steve Hill continued as an evangelist until his death in 2014.

keyMoments.text: Pastor John Kilpatrick begins Sunday-evening prayer meetings for revival at Brownsville Assembly of God.
Evangelist Steve Hill receives prayer from Sandy Millar at Holy Trinity Brompton in London.
On Father's Day Hill preaches at Brownsville; hundreds come forward and many fall, shake or weep.
Meetings are extended indefinitely and settle into four or five nights a week.
Michael Brown leads the newly formed Brownsville Revival School of Ministry.
The Pensacola News Journal publishes an investigative series questioning the revival's origins and finances.
Hill leaves, the school splits from the church, and the regular revival meetings wind down.
Kilpatrick leaves Brownsville to pursue a wider ministry.

experiences.significance: Brownsville was one of the largest and longest-running revivals in recent American history and the most prominent within a classical Pentecostal denomination, renewing an emphasis on repentance, conversion and the altar call alongside charismatic manifestations. Its ministry school sent hundreds of students into missions and church planting, and its music and preaching circulated widely on recordings. It also became a case study in the tensions of modern revival: claims of spontaneity versus planning, reported statistics, finances and media scrutiny. Supporters point to changed lives and lasting ministries, while critics question the manifestations and the commercial side of revival.

experiences.title: Asbury Outpouring

place.name: Hughes Auditorium, Asbury University, Wilmore, Kentucky

experiences.account: Paraphrase of university statements and news reports: after a routine student chapel service on 8 February 2023, a number of students stayed to pray, sing and confess sins. The gathering continued around the clock for about sixteen days, spreading by social media; tens of thousands of visitors (estimates around 50,000) queued to enter Wilmore, a town of about 6,000. Leaders deliberately avoided celebrity speakers, stage lighting and fund-raising, emphasising humility, confession and worship; some testified to healings. Public services ended on 23-24 February, with a gathering for young people.

primarySource.title: Asbury University public statements and press coverage, February 2023
primarySource.citation: Asbury University statements (February 2023); reports in Christianity Today, The New York Times and others

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Asbury had experienced similar extended chapel revivals in 1905, 1950 and 1970. Participants debated whether to call it a 'revival' or an 'outpouring' and worried about outside promotion and politicisation.

assessments.text: Seen as a renewal in the tradition of the Holiness movement, notable for its quietness and humility.
Welcomed as a sign of a wider awakening among Generation Z; some charismatic leaders sought to visit or promote it, prompting the university to ask for restraint.
Many welcomed the emphasis on confession and Scripture while urging caution about calling it revival before its long-term fruit is seen.
Observers linked it to post-pandemic loneliness and social media; its lasting impact is still under assessment.

debates: Revival vs. outpouring: how to define and measure.
Social media and the risk of spectacle.
experiences.story:
Asbury University is a small Christian liberal-arts college in Wilmore, Kentucky, a town of about 6,000 people south of Lexington. It belongs to the Wesleyan-Holiness tradition, and its history includes several extended 'revivals' in which ordinary chapel services continued for days, most famously in February 1970, when a service ran continuously for about a week and students then travelled across the United States to tell of it. Hughes Auditorium, its chapel, seats about 1,500.

On Wednesday, 8 February 2023, a regular morning chapel service took place. A visiting speaker preached on Romans 12 and the call to love in action, and the service closed with a song. According to students' and staff accounts, a group of around twenty students remained after the dismissal to keep praying and singing with the student worship team. Others drifted back. By the evening, word had spread through the campus that something unusual was happening, and the chapel began to fill.

The gathering continued around the clock. There was no main speaker. Students and others took turns leading songs, reading Scripture, praying for one another and giving testimonies of confession, reconciliation, and, in some cases, of healing. Videos and posts spread rapidly on social media, especially TikTok and Instagram, and within days visitors were arriving from across the United States and from other countries. Queues stretched through the town, sometimes for hours, and the university opened overflow venues, including other halls and nearby churches and the chapel of the neighbouring Asbury Theological Seminary. Estimates of the total number of visitors ranged from around 50,000 upwards.

University leaders and staff tried deliberately to keep the focus away from personalities. They avoided promoting celebrity preachers, kept the lighting and production simple, did not take offerings for the event, and emphasised humility, prayer, confession and the experience of the students themselves. President Kevin Brown and others described their role as stewarding rather than directing what was happening. Volunteers from the community provided food and practical help.

Not everyone was comfortable with the attention. Some participants and observers worried that visiting ministry figures and media would turn the gathering into a spectacle, that political or commercial interests might use it, and that the town could not cope with the crowds. Theologians and commentators debated whether to call it a 'revival', an 'outpouring' or simply an extended worship gathering, and cautioned that its significance could only be judged by its long-term effects. Similar extended worship gatherings were reported at several other Christian colleges in the weeks that followed.

On 17 February the university announced a plan to wind down the public services. A final large public gathering took place on 23 February, which coincided with the Collegiate Day of Prayer, and the following evening's service was reserved for people aged 25 and under. After that, regular chapel services resumed, and the university encouraged visitors to carry what they had experienced into their local churches.

keyMoments.text: A chapel service at Asbury College continues for about a week, the most famous of its earlier revivals.
After a routine chapel service, a group of students stays behind to pray and sing in Hughes Auditorium.
News spreads on social media and visitors begin arriving from across the United States.
Overflow venues open as queues stretch through Wilmore; estimates of visitors reach about 50,000.
The university announces plans to wind down public services.
A final large public service is held on the Collegiate Day of Prayer.
A last service is held for people aged 25 and under; normal chapel schedule resumes.

experiences.significance: The Asbury outpouring drew worldwide attention as a youth-led, low-production gathering in an era of large, technically polished worship events, and many saw it as a hopeful sign among Generation Z, a generation marked by high rates of anxiety and loneliness. Its leaders' deliberate refusal of celebrity and fund-raising became a model discussed by pastors and students elsewhere. It renewed debate over what counts as a revival, how social media both spreads and distorts such events, and how to measure lasting fruit. Historians place it within a long Wesleyan-Holiness tradition of campus revivals, and it is too early to judge its long-term effects on churches.
